title: Isak finally arrives as Gakpo proves value to Liverpool
description: Has the real Alexander Isak finally arrived at Liverpool after his two-goal display in their Premier League win at Ipswich Town, asks chief football writer Phil McNulty?
fullText:
Alexander Isak was the £125m striker who finally arrived at Liverpool by tormenting Ipswich Town - while Cody Gakpo's virtuoso performance had them giving thanks he never left.

The nuts and bolts of a comfortable Friday in Suffolk were that Liverpool won 2-0 - thanks to two Isak goals in the first nine minutes, giving them their first Premier League victory of the season and new manager Andoni Iraola's first since succeeding the sacked Arne Slot.

Liverpool's win must be placed in the context of being against a newly promoted Ipswich Town who were game, but who shipped five goals at Manchester United last week and look ripe for the picking against attacking quality.

The wider significance, however, was that Isak finally looked like the player Liverpool broke, at that time, the British transfer record to seal an acrimonious transfer from Newcastle United last summer.

Throw in the added bonus that Bradley Barcola showed flashes of devastating pace in a 26-minute debut display after his £123m arrival from Paris St-Germain, and this was a night that ticked every box for Iraola and Liverpool.

Even Barcola's bow, however, was overshadowed by Isak.

The Sweden striker looked a lost soul in his first season at Liverpool, arriving out of condition after downing tools to secure his move from Tyneside, then troubled by injuries as he gave the impression of being the most expensive vanity purchase in British football history.

He was outshone by fellow striker Hugo Ekitike, his statistics stark as he suffered along with many others in an astonishing decline amid Liverpool's dismal title defence that led to Slot's sacking only a year after he lifted the Premier League trophy.

Isak played 22 games encompassing 1,033 minutes, scoring four goals at a rate of one every 258 minutes. He played 14 games in the Premier League totalling 703 minutes, scoring only three goals at a rate of one every 234 minutes.

He has already equalled that league tally this season, but it was his demeanour as well as his lethal finishing that will have given Liverpool and Iraola confidence that the Isak code has finally been cracked.

And it was done by utilising Isak at his best - running in behind defenders and pressing with pace. It was what made him such a hot property at Newcastle United, and made everything about his every miserable moment on the pitch with Liverpool last term such a mystery.

It was also done in tandem with Gakpo, who could easily have been back in the north west preparing for Manchester City's game against Coventry City at Etihad Stadium had the move not collapsed.

Isak shines at last but Scherpen suffers - Ipswich v Liverpool player ratings

Gakpo was happy to join Enzo Maresca's Manchester City transition, but Liverpool's failure to sign Yankuba Minteh from Brighton or Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr meant he stayed at Anfield.

And it might just be one of those twists of fate football can throw up as Gakpo delivered a masterclass of creation that meant this game was effectively over after nine minutes.

Isak was the spearhead who delivered the defining moments, starting in the sixth minute when he took Gakpo's clever pass between Leif Davis and Jacob Greaves before thrashing a right-foot shot that carried too much power for Ipswich Town keeper Kjell Scherpen, although he had to do much, much better than divert the striker's effort into the net.

The second, three minutes later, was stamped right through with class, bringing a beaming smile to the face of Iraola.

Gakpo delivered a delicious pass with the outside of his right foot from inside his own half. Isak used a left-foot flick to move inside Greaves as Scherpen came out, before a touch with his right foot sent the Ipswich keeper the wrong way before rolling in a cool finish with his left.

Perfection from Gakpo's start to Isak's finish. Game over.

Isak had a desperately poor return to Tyneside on the opening day of the season, questions even coming about his performance after he scored in Liverpool's 2-2 draw at home to Nottingham Forest in their second game.

This, however, was Isak played right - and playing right.

Iraola said: "He's a massive player for us. My demands will probably not be about the goals. I know he is fit and in good shape. He's going to produce the numbers.

"My fight with him will be more about other stuff, how to help the team in other situations - but it is good he has already played two full games, scoring the goals, so I am very happy to have him."

And Isak added: "We were waiting for the first win. We talked about starting the game good, which we haven't done recently, so it was perfect for us to get two good quick goals.

"With a normal pre-season, I think we are starting to get to the way we want to play. To be offensive and attack the defence. I think we did that. We scored two, and we could have scored more."

Reflecting on his poor first season at Liverpool, Isak said: "It was not easy. It was obviously a long injury and a difficult season in general. I was thinking to have a good World Cup, and then to start off the season well, which I think I have done now. It's kind of behind me, but it wasn't easy."

Portman Road is certainly a happy hunting ground for Isak. Since the start of the 2024-25 season, his five Premier League goals there are the joint most by any player at an away ground, equalling Erling Haaland's haul against Crystal Palace at Selhurst Park.

Gakpo also struggled for his best form in the last campaign, but he has started this season in outstanding style. This was the elegant Netherlands forward at his best, not just by making two goals, but with his all-round performance.

Liverpool captain and compatriot Virgil van Dijk is certainly delighted to still be lining up alongside his team-mate for club and country, saying: "It's massive. I said it before the transfer window had closed.

"He's important for us, and he will be important this season. He showed it here. He showed it last week as well, and over the last couple of years. He needs to just keep going."

The same challenge now applies to Isak. Iraola will not want this to be a false dawn for such an exceptional talent that had lost his way.

title: Dean says he always applied laws - but which matches did he play games in?
description: Is there any evidence that former Premier League referee Mike Dean used to play mini-games during matches? BBC Sport has taken a look at the evidence.
fullText:
Former Premier League referee Mike Dean says he did not intend to "undermine the integrity of refereeing" after claiming that he used to play mini-games to amuse himself during matches.

Dean had told Jamie Vardy's podcast that he would try to go as long as possible without blowing his whistle, or stay standing in the centre circle.

"We used to say, 'we'll kick off now. Right, see how long we can go without blowing a whistle'," Dean said.

"I've done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR obviously - went 20, 25 minutes without blowing a whistle."

The 58-year-old has come in for considerable criticism for his comments with another former Premier League referee, Mark Halsey, telling BBC Sport that it had added extra pressure on officials today.

Dean posted a statement on his Instagram story on Friday where he did not retract his claim, but sought to explain the context.

"Throughout my 25 years as a professional referee, I have always applied the Laws of the Game to the best of my ability," Dean wrote.

"My approach as a referee was always to allow the game to flow and whenever possible I preferred to apply a high threshold for contact which the players liked.

"However, if I saw a foul challenge that needed me to take the appropriate action I would give it from the correct position.

"At no stage was it my intention to question, criticise or undermine the integrity of refereeing in this country.

"I have always respected the profession and the responsibility that comes with being a referee."

But is there any evidence that Dean did in fact play these games?

Halsey said it would be "impossible" to hold the whistle for just a few minutes, let alone more than 20.

So BBC Sport looked at the Premier League games officiated by Dean from 2008-09 until 2018-19, when the video assistant referee was introduced.

The focus was on more than 200 games that were 0-0 after 15 minutes, meaning there would be no need for a whistle for a kick off after a goal.

Are there any games which might provide evidence that Dean was playing around?

Only five such examples could be found, with no game reaching 20 minutes.

The longest was 18 minutes 50 seconds for a game involving West Brom and Man United, which Crystal Palace and Stoke at 18 minutes 20 seconds.

This did back up Dean's claim to have "a high threshold", with no clear evidence of obviously missed free-kicks.

Plenty of goals in this game, but Sunderland did not take the lead until deep into first-half stoppage time.

So, plenty of time for Dean to hold his whistle?

The game was 13 minutes 39 seconds old before the referee first needed to use the whistle.

The ball had gone out of play for a throw, and it looked like a Sunderland player was going to try to continue.

To be fair, not much had happened before that which warranted a whistle.

A Sunderland player was brought down on 11 minutes 21 seconds, which was definitely a foul, and Dean played an advantage.

It was a valid decision, but many officials may have stopped the game.

Another game which was uneventful with no foul or offside in the opening changes.

The match was 16 minutes 42 seconds old when Alejandro Faurlin was fouled and won a free-kick.

But would this match even count?

Dean did blow the whistle at six minutes 25 seconds because a throw-in was not taken in the right place.

Would this count as a breaker for Dean's little game?

This is the best example we were able to find, and the closest to Dean's claim he could go 20 minutes without blowing the whistle.

Sadio Berahino eventually won a free-kick for a foul by Daley Blind after 18 minutes 50 seconds.

No whistle was blown before this time.

Dean did let a few challenges go, and played an advantage at 18 minutes and 10 seconds, but nothing which would suggest he had deliberate not given a foul.

This might be the best example of Dean allowing the game to flow and not blowing his whistle.

It was 18 minutes 20 seconds in before he gave a free-kick for a foul on Stoke City's Ramadan Sobhi.

There was an incident on eight mins when he could have given a free-kick to Xherdan Shaqiri.

But other than that there was no case for a missed foul.

Dean finally blew his whistle at Selhurst Park after 16 minutes 3 seconds, awarding a free-kick to Hamza Choudhury.

That is a fair way into the match again, but not close of his claim to have go 20-25 minutes into a game without stopping it.

However, the referee blew the whistle on three minutes eight seconds to indicate a corner had been awarded. So it is difficult to say this one really counts.

title: Who are best Man City players to buy? FPL gameweek three dilemmas
description: BBC Sport FPL expert Gianni Buttice looks at some of the biggest dilemmas facing Fantasy Premier League managers heading into gameweek three.
fullText:
BBC Sport's FPL expert Gianni Buttice looks at some of the biggest dilemmas facing Fantasy Premier League managers heading into gameweek three.

If you do not own Erling Haaland (£15.5m), using a chip to bring him in is much simpler than spending several transfers to fit in the game's most expensive player.

A Wildcard lets you move quickly on trending players, improve team value, and invest heavily in two sides you may not have much exposure to in Manchester City and Chelsea, who face Coventry and Hull at home over the next fortnight.

The Free Hit chip also has an upside, allowing you to avoid the Arsenal versus Chelsea fixture and consider players from Brighton, Newcastle, and Brentford.

If you are not using a Wildcard or Free Hit, choosing Haaland as your Triple Captain looks a strong option, which I am likely to run with.

Coventry have been among the most defensively vulnerable sides and Manchester City impressed last time out, while their Norway striker has had a clear midweek before Saturday's game at Etihad Stadium.

City also host Ipswich in gameweek seven and Hull in gameweek 16, but both fixtures fall during heavy Champions League congestion.

Bruno Fernandes (£12.0m) faces Coventry at Old Trafford in gameweek 14, although that also comes in a run of three matches in seven days.

Rayan Cherki (£7.7m) is this week's most-bought player, with two price rises already. After his impressive last outing, he is the standout midfield pick.

Phil Foden (£7.0m) is also worth considering, with stronger underlying expected data than Cherki over the first two games, while Elliot Anderson (£6.4m) looks a solid long-term hold.

Cherki and Foden may become minutes risks later in the season, especially after the deadline-day signing of Enzo Fernández (£6.9m). In defence, Josko Gvardiol (£5.6m) is the best option.

The half-time substitution of Christos Tzolis against Aston Villa was a concern for owners.

We saw in gameweek one how dangerous he can be and many expect him to be first choice this season, albeit subject to early substitutions.

He's far from a hard sell though and arguably a comfortable hold at £6.5m.

Manchester United captain Fernandes is close to the ideal FPL asset: talismanic, takes set-pieces, rarely injured or substituted, and a reliable scorer.

He is a stronger option than Cole Palmer (£9.6m) or Bukayo Saka (£9.5m), but he is also significantly more expensive.

Because captaincy is so important, look ahead. if you are unlikely to captain Fernandes soon, but would give the armband to Palmer or Saka, the switch is worth considering.

It's also worth noting there are plenty of other good assets at Chelsea and Arsenal, whereas Fernandes is in a league of his own at United.

It is easy to be tempted by a new signing, but I would wait at least a week before buying anyone who has only just joined.

Most are unlikely to start this weekend and may be limited to cameo appearances. If they impress on debut, you can react then.

To name a few, I will be closely monitoring Daniel Munoz (£5.4m), Bradley Barcola (£8.0m), Jack Grealish (£6.5m), and the impact Fernandez will have on the minutes of other Manchester City midfielders.

title: Sutton's predictions v Kasabian frontman Serge Pizzorno
description: BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton takes on Kasabian frontman Serge Pizzorno, plus the BBC readers and AI with his predictions for this weekend's Premier League fixtures.
fullText:
Arsenal and Chelsea have both made 100% winning starts to the new season - but something has to give when they meet at Emirates Stadium on Sunday.

"I suspect Chelsea will give Arsenal lots of the ball and try to counter-attack quickly," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.

"The Blues have got some brilliant creativity in Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro, but the fact they are vulnerable at the back could undermine them."

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests.

For week three, he takes on Kasabian frontman Serge Pizzorno, who is a Leicester City fan.

Kasabian's ninth album, Act III, is out on Friday, 4 September, and they tour the UK in December.

It has been an eventful decade for Foxes fans since they won the Premier League title in 2016 - and not always an enjoyable one.

Since then, they have seen their side reach the Champions League quarter-finals, lift the FA Cup and Community Shield, win promotion from the Championship and suffer three relegations, including last season when they went down to League One.

"Promotion!" said Serge. "It has to be. I love the play-offs, so a win at Wembley would do me."

A new-look Leicester side took their first step towards bouncing back when they picked up their opening win of the season against Plymouth on Tuesday, but Serge added Russell Martin's youthful side will need time to fully find their feet in the third tier.

"I hope they get it," he said. "Patience is so important in football, and young teams should play with no fear."

Chris Sutton and Serge Pizzorno were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

My daughter's old maths teacher, Mr Fields, is an Ipswich fan and he is very excited about how ambitious the club has been since getting promoted. I think all their supporters must be the same.

Ipswich have spent almost £200m on a stack of new signings to try to stay in the Premier League and, watching them, it is clear they are not just planning to park the bus.

They will be confident for this game after beating Sunderland at home on the opening weekend and I am expecting them to have a real go at Liverpool too.

It will be interesting to see if new signing Bradley Barcola starts for the Reds, who seem to have a lot of attacking players who like to play off the left.

Boss Andoni Iraola has plenty of attacking options, but I still have concerns about them defensively, while his players adjust to his front-foot pressing style.

I am sure he will get it right eventually, but at the moment they are leaking goals and creaking at the back.

My gut feeling is Ipswich will score, but Liverpool will still edge the win after two successive 2-2 draws. If their attack clicks, it will be hard to keep them out.

Newcastle have started the season superbly with four points, and it feels like they have changed the mood at St James' Park after a difficult summer.

There's no doom and gloom about the place despite them losing several key players and, after predicting they would lose their first two games, I feel differently about their prospects now.

Things can change very quickly of course and a home defeat by Bournemouth would see a lot of that optimism disappear. But, so far, I've been really impressed by Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa looks like he has got his confidence back.

I like the way new manager Matthias Jaissle has set them up to hit teams on the counter-attack, and Nico Gonzalez looks like a sensible signing too.

I called Newcastle 'a development club' before their first game, because of the type of players they have bought and sold this summer, but while their midfield is quite youthful, they have now got Nico in there to give them a bit of extra clout.

This is still a tricky game to call, however.

Bournemouth haven't won yet, but only because they have let leads slip away late on, first against Manchester City and then at home to Everton.

Cherries boss Marco Rose is another manager who likes to play on the front foot and they are certainly capable of getting something here, even though I have gone for a home win.

I was spot on with my predictions for both of these teams last week, but I still don't feel very confident about calling the outcome of this game.

Brentford are a brilliant counter-attacking side who seem especially strong at home.

I was erring towards backing the Bees to win, like they did in this fixture last season, but then had second thoughts.

I backed the Black Cats to win their first two matches (see the table based on Sutton's predictions at the bottom of the page) because they are a well-organised team, with plenty of physicality and also a threat up top.

My concern for them is what happens when European football starts, but that hasn't happened yet. I don't see them losing this.

I am not really sure what to make of Brighton yet. They smashed Aston Villa on the opening weekend but then lost to Chelsea despite dominating possession in what was a really strange game.

Leeds can be quite cagey on the road under Daniel Farke, but they are very good at what they do, and they will be a threat on the break.

I am still going with Brighton to win because they are playing with freedom at the moment, but I don't see them keeping a clean sheet and this is going to be close.

Neither of these teams have got a point so far, as I predicted.

On top of his side's poor start to the season, one of the problems for Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage will be dealing with Ismaila Sarr after he did not get a move to Liverpool before the transfer window shut.

My worry for Fulham is they have become a Real Madrid feeder team, and their boss Alvaro Arbeloa has already got issues with his squad.

He stuck the boot into his players after their defeat by Sunderland, questioning their mentality.

A first win would be massive for both new managers, but I don't think either of them will get it here.

This is a tale of two Citys - one of whom has made the best of starts to the season, while the other has had the worst.

Manchester City wiped the floor with Crystal Palace last week but it was their comeback to beat Bournemouth at the Etihad which felt bigger, because it was the beginning of a new era under Enzo Maresca.

In contrast, Coventry City have had a terrible time. Not their 3-0 opening defeat at Arsenal, because they can forget about that, but they must feel so deflated after losing 1-0 at home to another promoted side in Hull last time out.

This game is more like the Arsenal one, in that no-one is expecting Coventry to get anything, but the upshot is they are likely to be left without a point or even a goal after their first three games.

There were some doubts about Manchester City after the way they lost the Community Shield against Arsenal, but they look a different proposition already.

Maresca has made more signings in the past few days, including Enzo Fernandez from his old club Chelsea for £125m. I've heard people question whether Fernandez is worth the big money that City paid, but Maresca knows him well and I see him as a great addition to their midfield.

I said before the Bournemouth game I didn't think they could win the title without Rodri, but they have rebuilt their midfield now with Fernandez and Ayyoub Bouaddi joining Elliot Anderson as new signings, and they have got real strength in there now.

I like Erling Haaland's new haircut too. It suits him far more than a ponytail. He looks a bit rougher and tougher and I don't think Coventry will keep him out.

Nottingham Forest are waiting for their first win under Oliver Glasner but I felt they were unlucky to lose against Leeds and also to only draw at Liverpool.

I have been very disappointed with Roberto de Zerbi's Tottenham so far, however, and not just because of their poor results.

When he came in at Brighton, De Zerbi built an amazing team in a short space of time and they were great to watch even if they made a few mistakes along the way.

In contrast, we still don't know what his Spurs team are about, even though they have spent an absolute fortune on players.

I think that's on De Zerbi because, although new players take time to gel, his side have put in two really insipid performances so far.

He has put that down to the team not being fully fit and blamed their pre-season schedule, but they should still be doing much better than they are - with no points and no goals so far.

Other clubs, with new managers as well as lots of new players, look much more organised so it is not an excuse.

Still, Spurs have surely got to improve soon, which is why I have got them down to pick up a first point here.

Hull will be on such a high after winning their first two games, and that makes this game even harder to predict.

The Tigers are really well organised and are not bothered about how much possession they have, they are just bothered about being effective when they do get the ball.

They defend the box brilliantly but there will still be a few weeks this season where teams run all over them because of the way they are set up.

Aston Villa won't necessarily do that, but I still think they will come out on top despite their poor start to the new campaign.

Ollie Watkins is a big loss but they have got Nicolas Jackson in to lead their line, who I think is a good signing.

It took Villa six games to register their first league win last season, but they won't have to wait as long this time.

Everton ended up keeping hold of young midfielder Harrison Armstrong but they made a mess of their attempts to sign another striker before the transfer window closed.

I know Thierno Barry comes in for criticism and his finishing is erratic, but at least they still have him to lead their line.

He scores some brilliant goals too, as does Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, so I don't think it will be all doom and gloom for Everton fans this season, despite their frustration at the moment.

As for Manchester United, well I know some of their supporters think I am down on them all the time.

So, I'd like to point out I backed them to win their first two games of the season and they are joint top of the table (below) based on my predictions.

This time, I'm going for a draw, but that would still be a decent result for Michael Carrick's side.

Arsenal were a bit clunky last time out against Aston Villa, while I love what Xabi Alonso is doing at Chelsea.

He doesn't care about possession, and that's not how Chelsea try to get results.

It's strange because I had a look at how his Bayer Leverkusen side lined up when they won the Bundesliga, and they were pretty dominant possession-wise.

So, it is quite alarming when you look at the two league games Chelsea have played and see how much of the ball they haven't had. Against Fulham they only had 38% possession and then against Brighton it was down to 25%.

I don't know whether that is by design or by just not having the players to dominate. They are still free-scoring, but they are conceding loads of goals too.

Whatever the reason, I don't see it changing here. Arsenal are so powerful and the only question mark around them is if they are a forward or two short.

Even so, you would not exactly say they have a real weakness anywhere. The beauty of Mikel Arteta's side is they can play in different ways.

They demolished Manchester City in the Community Shield with some pure football, and played some nice stuff against Coventry too, but then they were able to grind out a win at Aston Villa as well.

Ultimately, whether they are free-flowing or not, their organisation should see them through this game too.

Chris picked up his first win of the season after getting seven correct results - including three exact scores - from the 10 matches in week two.

After a slow start, five of his correct results - and two of his exact scores - came in the five games on Sunday and Monday.

That gave him a total of 160 points, enough to hold off a strong challenge from the BBC readers and AI.

The collective efforts of the readers helped them get six correct results, with two exact scores, for 120 points.

Like Chris, AI managed seven correct results, but with only one exact score, leaving it on 100 points.

Chris' guest, Royal Blood drummer Ben Thatcher, did not fare so well. He got four correct results with no exact scores, and ended up with 40 points.

"It's not how you start the weekend, it's how you finish it," Sutton said. "I am burying AI at the moment, which is a lovely feeling."

Everyone was right about three of the fixtures - Manchester City's win at Crystal Palace, Manchester United's victory over Ipswich and Arsenal's success at Aston Villa.

There were only two fixtures where none of our predictors picked the right outcome - Liverpool's draw with Nottingham Forest and Hull's win at Coventry.

From almost 37,000 predictions for the latter, only around 5,000 (15%) of you backed the Tigers to take the three points, and fewer than 1,500 (4%) went for them to win by a 1-0 scoreline.

title: Will De Zerbi Make Any Changes? | 4-2-3-1 Tottenham Hotspur Predicted Lineup Vs Nottingham Forest
description: Tottenham Hotspur will lock horns with Nottingham Forest at the City Ground on Saturday as they look to secure a good result on the road in the Premier League. Spurs suffered a poor 2-0 loss at the ha...
fullText:
Tottenham Hotspur will lock horns with Nottingham Forest at the City Ground on Saturday as they look to secure a good result on the road in the Premier League. Spurs suffered a poor 2-0 loss at the hands of Newcastle United recently, so they would be eager to bounce back by securing a win this weekend.

Roberto De Zerbi will set his side up in a 4-2-3-1 formation and is expected to keep changes to a minimum for this game. Therefore, Omar Marmoush could get another chance to impress as a centre-forward for the North London club up top.

title: Swansea on the way to reviving style - Matos
description: Vitor Matos believes Swansea are reviving the possession game which was key to the club's golden period in the Premier League.
fullText:
Vitor Matos believes his Swansea City side are on the way to reviving the sort of stylish possession game which was key to the club's golden period in the Premier League.

Swansea are top of the early Championship table having banked 10 points from their first four league games.

The Swans host Wrexham in a mouthwatering Welsh derby on Saturday having produced one of the club's best performances in recent memory as they overcame Watford in midweek.

Head coach Matos believes his new-look team are moving towards playing the sort of eye-catching football Swansea became known for under the likes of Roberto Martinez, Brendan Rodgers and Michael Laudrup.

"Swansea always had a style. When you closed your eyes and you started thinking about Swansea and what that style is and what the DNA of the club is, you got some images in your mind," he said.

"My view and my idea was always that we need to get as close to that as possible to again build back that DNA, to use that to try to link everyone properly, to create a connection between everyone at the club.

"We are on the way, we see moments of that."

Matos suggested when he took charge in November 2025 that Swansea had moved away from the style which brought success following the appointment of Martinez as manager of the then third-tier club in 2007.

title: London City shirt deal biggest in women's game & beats some in Premier League - Kang
description: London City Lionesses owner Michele Kang says they have signed the biggest shirt sponsorship deal in the women's game.
fullText:
London City Lionesses owner Michele Kang says her club's new shirt sponsorship deal with sports brand Nike is the largest in the women's game - and worth more than those of some Premier League sides.

The current largest deal for a women's side is believed to be for the new National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) franchise in Atlanta, which is set to join the competition in 2028.

Atlanta's shirt deal is reportedly worth about $4m (£2.96m), a similar figure to that of new entrants to the Premier League and more than most Championship clubs.

"I can absolutely confirm that this is the largest women-only front-of-shirt deal," Kang told BBC Sport. "It is higher than the Atlanta number.

"I can absolutely also share that it is higher than some of the men's Premier League front-of-shirt deals. It's huge. That's why it's landmark."

The news comes after a big summer for London City which has seen them sign two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas and Spain defender Mapi Leon from Barcelona, as well as ex-England goalkeeper Mary Earps and Lyon winger Kadidiatou Diani.

London City's record is only for independent women's clubs, of which they are the only one in England's top flight.

Kang took over London City in 2023 and has shaken up the WSL, spending heavily to get the team to the top flight. They then finished sixth in the division last year.

title: Spurs omit Richarlison from Premier League squad

title: The Premier League premium is £20m - and that worries European clubs
description: The old adage used to be that English players came at a premium. Now that appears to simply apply to a player already in the Premier League.
fullText:
The old adage used to be that English players came at a premium. Now that appears to simply apply to a player already in the Premier League.

As English football set a host of new records for spending in the summer window, the average spend on a player signed from another Premier League club was £39.4m - almost double the £20.2m spent on those arriving from abroad.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, calls it "a Premier League tax".

It is part a growing trend which has seen Premier League teams become increasingly comfortable with selling to each other, even rivals.

While more total spending is done with clubs outside of England, the proportion of big-money domestic deals is now outstripping overseas transfers.

Only the European elite can now compete with Premier League clubs, and player profits are key when it comes to recycling money to keep in line with the financial rules.

Spending patterns for Premier League clubs are not just about the fee, but who the clubs are choosing to do business with.

Take a look at the high-value deals, worth £40m or more, which have doubled this summer from two years ago.

In 2024-25 there were 13 such deals, this summer there were 27.

More striking is the breakdown of these transfers.

Two years ago, there were seven transfers worth £40m or more done with teams on the continent. Only six were completed between Premier League clubs.

This summer there were nine deals worth £40m or more with European clubs.

But between clubs in England it has trebled, from six to 18. The total spend across all domestic transfers has more than doubled, too.

Maguire told BBC Sport that one reason is English clubs now scout players from abroad so extensively that they are signed much earlier, and made into Premier League players.

"We've got a new tranche of clubs, sort of the the algorithm kids, who are recruiting from the international markets," Maguire said.

"They're bringing players to the Premier League, and then the Big Six clubs are signing the best players."

On such example is Carlos Baleba, who Brighton signed from Lille three years ago for £23m and last week sold to Manchester United for £70m.

"It has effectively created a recruitment area, sort of a petri dish, to determine which of the overseas players can deliver in the Premier League, and then it's a win-win for all the parties," Maguire added.

But that only tells part of the story. There are also the transfers which look like they could only happen in the Premier League.

Would a European club have given Manchester City the £75m Tottenham spent on Savio? Or paid Everton £65m for Iliman Ndiaye? What about the £85m West Ham received from Spurs for Mateus Fernandes?

As if to underline this, only seven signings of £40m or more were made this summer by European clubs, from another on the continent, all by Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Paris St-Germain.

Trevor Watkins, the former Bournemouth chairman who now works as a sports lawyer, told BBC 5 Live Breakfast that the Premier League almost operates within its own bubble.

"The revenues dwarf what other leagues generate," Watkins said. "And what you see this year is a lot of deals between clubs in England.

"A lot of money going down to lower leagues, but also between Premier League sides because, to be honest, they're probably the only ones that will pay the wages or pay the fees."

The transfer market appears to have become a game of spreadsheets where it is almost impossible to value players against each other.

The reason is simple, but the explanation more complicated.

Profit on a transfer is in some ways more significant than a player's worth in saves, clearances, assists or goals. Because profit enables reinvestment in the squad.

Let's try to set out how it works.

Elliot Anderson cost Nottingham Forest £35m from Newcastle, and they sold him for £116m. But that is not a profit of £81m.

The original transfer fee is averaged over the length of his Forest contract, and when he moved to Manchester City around £21m was left on the books.

Under the Premier League's new squad cost ratio (SCR) rules, that is a profit of £95m which is averaged over three years, at £31.67m for Forest.

Clubs can no longer sell a player for a one-hit quick fix - either to boost spending power in one window or to avert breaches of the financial regulations.

Why does this matter? It makes it even more important for clubs to generate high transfer fees, to get a higher profit average for SCR - which itself is calculated over one season.

But SCR undoubtedly benefits the biggest clubs with the greatest financial power.

The 'Big Six' - Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Tottenham - with their commercial revenues on a completely different scale, spent £1.658bn on players.

"Those clubs have future-proofed themselves by trying to generate more income," Maguire said. "Spurs is a classic example. Spurs now have a multi-function, multi-sport stadium, of which the football club is the biggest part.

"It is a reward for those clubs that have expanded their stadiums, or thought outside of the box in terms of trying to generate additional revenues."

For the other 14 clubs, who in total spent £1.833bn, player trading is crucial.

Between them, Aston Villa and Newcastle completed five deals worth £40m or more, but only after they brought in hundreds of millions of pounds from player sales.

If Premier League clubs are spending more of their money between themselves, that means less is flowing onto the continent.

But there are fears that this will still act as an inflationary trigger for fees and wages across the continent.

On Wednesday, Javier Gomez, La Liga's corporate general director, criticised the "loss-making model which is an issue exclusive to the Premier League".

"It has other consequences," Gomez said. "It inflates the entire sector - it inflates the Premier League, the Bundesliga, the French League, and eventually us as well."

Some of Europe's traditionally bigger teams have already found themselves no long able to compete with the top teams in the Premier League.

"With the exception of some of the global brands within football, and I think you'd look at Real Madrid, Barcelona, PSG and Bayern Munich, the Premier League can outspend anyone and everyone," Maguire said.

"We've seen that in the recent Deloitte Money League,, external with 14 teams from the Premier League in the 30 biggest teams in world football."

Real, Barca, PSG and Bayern are the top four on that list with Liverpool leading the six English clubs that fill out the top 10.

Andre Villas-Boas, the president of FC Porto, told BBC Sport that the Portuguese club has had to step up their scouting efforts instead of getting into bidding wars they cannot win.

"For Porto, it means we are competing for talent not with Man City or Liverpool but with (the likes of) Coventry and Brentford, without any disrespect," Villas-Boas said.

"The fact that they have this spending power makes it difficult for us.

"The Premier League is set apart from all the rest, which means English clubs are becoming more and more dominant of European competitions."

Aston Villa and Crystal Palace won the Europa League and Conference League respectively last season, while Arsenal were beaten by Paris St-Germain in the final of the Champions League.

The Premier League's transfer spending is the bubble which just refuses to burst.

And it risks creating further inequalities in European football.

title: I used to play in-match games as a laugh - Dean
description: Former Premier League referee Mike Dean says he would stay in the centre circle for as long as he could during a match.
fullText:
Former Premier League referee Mike Dean says he used to set himself mini-challenges during matches "as a laugh".

Appearing on Jamie Vardy's podcast, Dean said he would see how long he could go without blowing his whistle, or stay inside the centre circle.

"We used to say, 'we'll kick off now. Right, see how long we can go without blowing a whistle'," he added.

"I've done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR obviously - went 20, 25 minutes without blowing a whistle.

"I used to do another thing. I used to stand in the centre circle - see how long I could stay in the centre circle before I had to leave.

"That was just me joking about. I got about 15 minutes once."

Mark Halsey, who refereed in the Premier League between 1999 and 2013, told BBC Sport that Dean's comments damaged the reputation of all referees.

BBC Sport understands that refereeing figures consider Dean's claims to be unfounded, which would be historical and go back to the pre-video assistant referee era before 2019, when Pro Ref was under different leadership.

It is not the first time he has courted controversy for his media statements.

When acting as the video assistant referee (VAR) for Chelsea's 2-2 draw with Tottenham in August 2022, Dean failed to send the referee to the monitor for a red card for Cristian Romero.

The Spurs defender should have been penalised for pulling Marc Cucurella's hair.

After retiring, Dean said in an interview he did not intervene because he wanted to save referee Anthony Taylor from extra "grief".

"I didn't want to send him up because he is a mate as well as a referee," he revealed.

Dean enjoyed a 28-year career as a professional official, stepping down from on-field officiating in 2022 and retiring after spending the 2022-23 season as a full-time VAR.

The 58-year-old began officiating in 1985 and progressed from refereeing in the Football League 10 years later, and then to Premier League in 2000.

Dean refereed the 2008 FA Cup final and 2011 League Cup final at Wembley.

Halsey also doubted Dean's story was true, but he had questions to answer if so.

"It's caused so much controversy, and in all my years as a professional referee I have never heard of these these games, never," said Halsey.

"If Mike has played these games, then he's done that of his own accord.

"And if he has, then I think we need to know what games he's done them in, and how many games he's done them in. It brings into question the integrity of every official now."

Halsey added he had spoken to other officials today who said "they've not heard of it either", as he questioned the validity of Dean's claims.

"It's just impossible to go five minutes, let alone 20 minutes, without blowing your whistle to giving a free-kick," he said.

When Dean said in 2023 that he had helped out "a mate" in the Chelsea-Tottenham game from a year earlier, it caused real damage to the reputation of referees.

Officials have to deal with baseless allegations of corruption and favouritism as it is, so giving any kind of credence to a lack of professionalism by a referee is a problem.

As one serving referee told me at the time, it was as though Dean had "thrown them all under a bus". It tars everyone with the same brush, regardless of the facts.

Dean's revelations this week are not quite so explosive, and it is difficult to know whether, if true, they could have an impact on a game.

Of course, if Dean refused to blow his whistle to give a penalty because he was playing one of these games, that is a different matter.

But without Dean giving any specific examples, it could equally be the case that he was trying to make himself come across as 'one of the boys' when chatting with ex-players.

After making the claim, comedian and podcast co-host Josh James jokingly said to Dean: "Easy money."

Refereeing bosses consider Dean to be of the old school, a different era when the organisation may not have been quite so professional and progressive.

But even though it is more than four years since Dean stepped out onto a football pitch he remains as well-known as most current referees.

And when he says something controversial, it is going to get traction.

title: Ranking the most game-changing transfers in Premier League history
description: Some transfers take time to bed in, others prove instant game-changers - here are the top 10 signings of the Premier League era that moved the needle.
fullText:
The 'here we go' is on hold, the 'bombas' are done and dusted and the window panes are reverberating after being forcefully closed on Tuesday night.

Now comes the moment for new arrivals to make their mark on the pitch rather than the balance sheet.

Throughout the Premier League era there have been hordes of transfer hits and misses, but today we're looking at those signings who proved game-changing for their club and the competition, the ones who really moved the needle.

I've ranked my top 10 below. You can have your say in the comments.

You could make an argument for plenty of players who were left off this list. Thierry Henry is probably the one quibbled over the most, Arsene Wenger turning him from misfiring winger to one of the generation's greatest forwards.

But Arsenal had been champions 12 months before he arrived, and it took until Henry's third season for the Gunners to reclaim that crown.

You could point to Cristiano Ronaldo, who won a Ballon d'Or at Manchester United, or Wayne Rooney, who became the club's record goalscorer.

But a teenage Ronaldo took time to bed in, while Rooney, despite a debut hat-trick in Europe, had to wait until his third season for a Premier League winners' medal.

Then there's a plethora of Manchester City signings. Erling Haaland announced himself with 36 goals in 35 top-flight games but arrived in the middle of City's four-year title-winning streak. Yaya Toure, Kevin de Bruyne and Rodri all had big impacts.

However, the list can only be 10 names long. So here it is...

10. Petr Cech - Rennes to Chelsea, £7m, July 2004

Austrian goalkeeper Jurgen Macho was one of first faces through the door as the Roman Abramovich era began at Chelsea, arriving on a free transfer from Sunderland, only to tear his cruciate ligament and never play for the club.

A keeper signed the following summer would prove far more influential at Stamford Bridge.

While prising Claude Makelele from Real Madrid's Galacticos was a huge statement - likewise Hernan Crespo from Inter Milan - Petr Cech was the wall on which back-to-back titles were built.

Cech conceded only 15 goals in his debut league campaign, going on a run of 1,025 minutes without being beaten and ending the season with a record 24 clean sheets.

His Chelsea career spanned 11 seasons and included four Premier League titles and a Champions League. The Blues made back the £7m they paid - and then some.

9. Alan Shearer - Southampton to Blackburn, £3.6m, July 1992

Blackburn Rovers, fresh off a sixth-placed finish in Division Two, immediately set out their intentions after promotion via the play-offs guaranteed them a spot in the inaugural Premier League season.

Southampton striker Alan Shearer had interest from Manchester United, but Rovers - bankrolled by local businessman Jack Walker - tabled a British record £3.6m for the 21-year-old and enjoyed an almost immediate return.

Shearer scored 16 times in his first 21 Premier League games before injury, helping Blackburn finish fourth in their first top-flight season for 27 years. He bagged 31 as they finished runners-up the following term, and 34 in 1994-95 as Rovers were crowned champions for the first time since 1914.

Chris Sutton, another British record buy at £5m from Norwich City, may argue he was the signing who got Blackburn over the line, forming a formidable 'SAS' frontline, but it was Shearer's arrival that set the ball rolling.

8. Carlos Tevez - Corinthians to West Ham, undisclosed, August 2006

West Ham fans frantically refreshing Ceefax on 31 August 2006 must have thought they'd landed on the jokes page when news broke of a double swoop for a pair of Argentina's top young stars.

It was a huge coup for the Hammers, pipping the world's best clubs to add 22-year-olds Carlos Tevez and Javier Mascherano to Alan Pardew's squad.

With West Ham struggling near the bottom of the league, Mascherano left for Liverpool on loan after Christmas. Tevez, meanwhile, would have a huge impact.

West Ham were bottom with 11 games to go - nine points adrift of Sheffield United - but won seven games and Tevez netted seven times, including the winner against Manchester United on the final day, to relegate the Blades.

Sheffield United claimed foul play over the third-party ownership of Tevez and Mascherano, and West Ham were eventually ordered to pay £20m in compensation, having initially been fined £5.5m rather than being docked points.

7. Robinho - Real Madrid to Manchester City, £32.5m, August 2008

It gets somewhat lost in the cloudy narrative of the past, but Robinho had a decent first season at Manchester City, scoring on his Premier League debut and netting 14 times in 31 top-flight games to finish as their top scorer.

Things went downhill from there, but Robinho's performance was less important than what his arrival meant for the future of English football. It was City laying down a marker.

On the day the club were bought by the Abu Dhabi United Group - it also happened to be transfer deadline day - they nabbed one of the world's most prominent players from under the noses of Chelsea for a British record fee.

City finished 10th that season. But 18 years and more than £3bn on transfers later, they have become the most dominant club in England, winning eight titles.

6. Virgil van Dijk, Southampton to Liverpool, £75m, January 2018

Mohamed Salah might feel hard done by here. After all, he did score 32 Premier League goals in his first season at Liverpool after arriving from Roma in 2017.

But that didn't immediately move the needle in terms of pushing Liverpool further up the league table - they finished fourth again and scored only six more goals as a team compared to the previous season.

Instead, it was the £75m signing of Virgil van Dijk in January 2018 - and arguably goalkeeper Alisson Becker that summer too - that really raised the bar for Jurgen Klopp's side, who lost only once the following season and conceded only 22 goals as they racked up 97 points.

Incredibly, Liverpool were beaten to the title by Manchester City, but they became European champions and the following season won a first league title in 30 years.

5. Robin van Persie, Arsenal to Manchester United, £22.5m, August 2012

It was a sign of how the Manchester United and Arsenal rivalry had cooled.

Once the key protagonists in Premier League heavyweight contests, the Gunners would seemingly never contemplate allowing their top scorer to join United.

Yet on the back of a season in which he netted 30 goals to finish as the league's top scorer, Robin van Persie left Arsene Wenger's outfit to line up for Sir Alex Ferguson, who was scorned by Manchester City's emergence and desperate to return the title to Old Trafford.

Van Persie went on to score 26 times as United reclaimed the throne in Ferguson's final season - the club's 20th title - while Arsenal slipped to a distant fourth.

4. Sol Campbell, Tottenham to Arsenal, free transfer, July 2001

A handful of journalists gathered at Arsenal's London Colney training base expecting the unveiling of goalkeeper Richard Wright from Ipswich. Instead they were stunned to see former Tottenham skipper Sol Campbell walk in.

The England defender, who joined Spurs as a youngster more than a decade earlier, had lucrative offers from Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Inter Milan.

There was no inkling that he would end up down the road at Highbury instead, the deal sealed during clandestine meetings with Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger and vice-chairman David Dein.

"I have kept my head when other people around me were losing it," Campbell said at the unveiling of a transfer that was both seismic in the north London rivalry and the direction of the Premier League trophy.

He proved a phenomenal presence at the heart of Arsenal's defence, winning the league and FA Cup double that season and adding another Premier League crown as one of the 'Invincibles' two years later - a title clinched, of all places, at White Hart Lane.

3. N'Golo Kante, Caen to Leicester, £5.6m, August 2015

N'Golo Kante was playing in France's regional amateur leagues until his late teens. Only three years before he joined Leicester City in 2015, the tireless midfielder was turning out in his country's third tier.

The Foxes thought they'd found a bargain, but did not realise quite what an impact his arrival would have.

Kante became the beating heart of Claudio Ranieri's midfield as Leicester went on their astonishing title-winning run. While Jamie Vardy scored the goals and Riyad Mahrez brought the flair, it was the diminutive Frenchman's energy and ability to always be in the right place that set the tone.

Kante missed only one game and made more tackles and interceptions than anyone in the division on his way to becoming a Premier League champion, before Chelsea paid the Foxes almost five times what they nabbed him from Caen for a year earlier.

2. Sergio Aguero, Atletico Madrid to Manchester City, £35m, July 2011

Sergio Aguero set out on his debut as he meant to go on, scoring twice and setting up another in a 30-minute cameo off the bench against Swansea City.

Manchester City were without a top-flight title since 1968 when the Argentine arrived from Atletico Madrid.

Ten months later he had netted 23 goals in 34 Premier League games, including the one deep into stoppage time that crowned City champions.

City had spent lavishly on forwards previously but the prolific Aguero was a game-changer.

His goals shifted the power balance in Manchester and, after a decade in sky blue, he departed as the club's all-time record scorer with 260 goals to complement his five league titles.

1. Eric Cantona, Leeds United to Manchester United, £1.6m, November 1992

Where do you start with Eric Cantona? The maverick Frenchman arrived in England having won the title with Marseille, which was followed by a two-month ban for throwing a ball at a referee and a fallout with the hierarchy.

Advised to move to England, he rocked up at Leeds in January 1991 and swiftly helped them clinch the First Division.

A few months into the new season, Cantona's relationship with manager Howard Wilkinson broke down.

Manchester United, languishing in mid-table by late November, without a league title in 26 years and having been dumped out of the Uefa Cup by Torpedo Moscow, came calling - after their bid for Wednesday striker David Hirst was rejected.

Cantona proved a revelation. He scored nine times in 23 games and was influential as United ended up winning the inaugural Premier League title by 10 points.

The forward would win four titles in five years at Old Trafford, including two league and cup doubles, laying the foundations for a generation of success before his shock retirement in 1997.

title: Man City buy costly new midfield - but have they overlooked Haaland cover?
description: Manchester City have completed a squad overhaul including a fully revamped midfield to the tune of a Premier League record £458m, but that eyewatering number does not tell the full story.
fullText:
Manchester City have completed their squad overhaul - including a fully revamped midfield - to the tune of £458m, a new Premier League record for a summer window.

But that eyewatering sum does not tell the full story.

New Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca received the full backing of director of football Hugo Viana in his first transfer window in charge after replacing Pep Guardiola. Indeed, City's record transfer fee was twice broken this summer.

A joint-British record £125m was spent on Maresca's former Chelsea skipper Enzo Fernandez after £116m was committed on Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest. Morocco international Ayyoub Bouaddi, 18, was also brought in for £86m. The trio accounted for the bulk of City's summer incomings.

The departures of captain Bernardo Silva, 2024 Ballon d'Or winner Rodri, Tijjani Reijnders and Nico Gonzalez means the City midfield has been completely transformed.

Senior club sources are said to be delighted by the business done not only during the past couple of months but in January too, when plans were brought forward to sign long-term targets Antoine Semenyo and Marc Guehi.

And if the clock is rewound further back, Manchester City's rebuild of the team that won the 2023 Champions League really began in January 2025 after a difficult start to that season.

Just four players remain from the starting eleven and substitutes from the night they beat Inter Milan in Istanbul to win the continent's biggest club prize.

Maresca now has the luxury of calling upon two established players in almost every position. City feel the squad is stronger at this point than at the beginning of last season which they believe has been achieved by remaining calm and trusting the transfer strategy.

However some big questions remain.

How will their new midfield signings all fit together?

And, despite the vast amount of money spent, have they actually left themselves without a back-up to Erling Haaland?

Deadlines, acrimony and a record as Man City back Maresca for Fernandez deal

Ndiaye's journey from non-league football to £65m Man City move

City's expenditure of £542m on new signings since the turn of the year will grab the headlines, but it often goes under the radar how well they do at selling fringe players.

During this same period, they have recouped £334m, including £75m for Savinho, who scored only two Premier League goals during his time at City, as well as £65m for Rodri and £52m for Reijnders.

It gives City a net spend of £208m in 2026, which will be further bolstered by Tottenham's obligation to buy Omar Marmoush for £60m at the end of his loan spell next season.

Sources had said during the summer that they were operating on a one-out, one-in policy and Maresca managed to replace almost every player that departed, aside from Nico Gonzalez and Marmoush.

With the side well stocked at left-back, it is felt that Nico O'Reilly will play 

The club believe the record fee for Fernandez is justified by acquiring a proven winner at the highest level that will strengthen the midfield. Anderson was the summer's number one target, while 18-year-old Bouaddi is seen as having all the attributes to develop into a world class talent.

City have won back-to-back games at the start of the Premier League season and Maresca will now have a selection dilemma each game as he possesses an embarrassment of riches to choose from.

The question is how the Italian will now fit them all together.

Fernandez, Bouaddi, and Anderson are all players comfortable across multiple positions in Maresca's system.

Maresca has moved between a box and a diamond shape in midfield at City. The main difference between the two shapes is that the former has two natural holding midfielders and the second a single holding midfielder.

Against Bournemouth, Guehi paired Anderson at the base of midfield. O'Reilly, the left-sided attacking midfielder, was joined by right-back Rico Lewis, moving in-field to form the box.

Against Crystal Palace, left-back Josko Gvardiol and attacking midfielder O'Reilly flanked number 10 Rayan Cherki as the three ahead of Anderson in what looked like a diamond.

Anderson anchoring the midfield suggests Maresca sees him as Rodri's successor.

While full of praise for Bouaddi, Maresca has stressed his youth, a nod to the fact that he will likely deputise for Anderson.

Bouaddi replaced Anderson against Palace and his short cameo came soon after the introduction of Mateo Kovacic. In pre-season, the Croatian appeared to be Maresca's first choice holding midfielder but has since slid down the pecking order.

When he came on, although starting higher than Bouaddi in the midfield diamond, he dropped deep to get on the ball in holding midfield. When this happened, Bouaddi took Kovacic's position higher up.

These rotations between holding midfield and central midfield are movements Maresca may also encourage Anderson to perform when others fill the space behind him.

Versatility in the midfield four is key. Fernandez, under Maresca, was capable of playing at the base of midfield or as an attacking midfielder on both sides.

The last midfield spot, the number 10 position, has been shared between Foden and Cherki. Although Foden did play right wing against Bournemouth and Palace given City's injuries, Maresca has spoken of his central quality.

Given Foden's promising showings as a box-to-box midfielder last season – there is also a possibility both him and Cherki play through the middle together at some point this season.

Despite the positives around the recent window, Haaland is now City's only first-team striker.

The 26-year-old is pivotal to the team, ending last season as the Premier League top scorer with 27 goals, and starting the new campaign by netting twice in as many games.

But should Haaland be unavailable, what are City's options?

Marmoush wanted to play regular first-team football and was allowed to join Tottenham, while 21-year-old Divin Mubama, who did well in pre-season, joined Championship side Southampton on loan.

City believe they have enough flexibility from within their options to have not directly replaced Marmoush.

Semenyo operates mainly from the right flank but is seen as an option at number nine, having played in the position during some cup games last season.

Deadline day signing Ndiaye is another who can operate there and the £60m forward adds greater versatility and squad depth as someone who is a proven Premier League player.

However, of the forward, attacking midfield and wide options, Semenyo is the only one to get into double figures in the Premier League in the last couple of seasons.

Cherki, Jeremy Doku and Ndiaye have never hit that mark, while Foden is clearly capable, having hit 19 Premier League goals in 2023-24, but has struggled for consistent form in the last two seasons

Unless a couple of those step up, it could be one to watch if Haaland either needs to be rested or gets injured.

title: Monaco CEO breaks down Folarin Balogun's failed Everton deadline day transfer
description: AS Monaco CEO Thiago Scuro has gone into detail about U.S. Men's National Team striker Folarin Balogun's failed deadline day transfer to Premier League side Everton
fullText:
U.S. Men's National Team striker Folarin Balogun's prospective return to the Premier League is off after the 25-year-old former Arsenal academy star pulled out of a move to Everton at the last minute.

Tuesday at 11pm BST (5pm ET) marked the deadline in the English summer transfer window, and despite a last gasp effort to secure Balogun's signature by the Toffees, which would have netted AS Monaco some much-needed funds, the deal ultimately fell through in dramatic fashion.

Speaking with reporters on Wednesday after the dust had settled, Monaco CEO Thiago Scuro gave a fascinating insight into exactly what went wrong on Tuesday between the clubs and Balogun, and what the future may hold for the World Cup star - who was at the center of one of the tournament's biggest controversies.

Admitting that the club's approach to the summer market was to raise funds in order to meet financial regulations, he commented, via Get The Football News France, "Clearly, we were open to discussing and finding a transfer for Balogun. He finished his third season. We had already worked in advance to replace him, and we were fully ready to do this. Things went very well with this strategy until we were almost there."

Since joining Monaco in 2023 from Arsenal, following loan stints with Middlesbrough and Reims, Balogun has found the back of the net 31 times in 91 games, providing a further 13 assists along the way in all competitions. Last season was particularly fruitful for the forward, scoring 19 goals in 43 appearances.

But with the club in need of funds and Balogun two years away from hitting free agency, Monaco clearly felt it was the right time to cash in, not naming him to any of their matchday squads so far this season and, ultimately, attempting to ship him off to Merseyside.

"During the day, we had a clear agreement for Balogun to go to Everton. Balogun flew yesterday morning to go for medicals and sign a contract," Scuro said. "Our plan worked very well in this moment in terms of revenue generation, squad planning, player transfers.

"Thilo [Kehrer] going (to Ajax), as announced, opened the space in the salary that we needed with the DNCG (French football's financial watchdog). Balogun, besides the salary, was also an important source of income for the club, which would help us also to balance the season."

To listen to the latest episode of 'All Out Soccer' - CLICK HERE

However, things began to unravel on Tuesday evening, as Scuro detailed. "Around 7 pm, we were contacted by Everton, raising questions about Balogun's medical, which, for our medical staff, as well as for the player's personal medical staff, made no sense at all," he said.

"The explanations were not enough to justify or to bring concerns regarding the future of the player, which there aren't. This discussion started between medical departments from here and there.

"It took Everton around 2-3 hours to go deep into the assessment and check with other doctors. This is a normal situation when the doctor of the club raises concerns. It's quite normal that clubs will look for other specialists, share the images and discuss the case. This was ongoing."

Around three hours passed by which point Everton gave the move the green light. However, in need of more time to finalize the deal, the teams triggered a Premier League rule allowing for an extension of an hour to complete a last-minute move.

"The Premier League has a mechanism in which you can request one extra hour to finish the paperwork. This was done," he said. "Five minutes to close the transfer window there, for us to finish all the paperwork between Monaco and Everton and 'Balo'. I signed the contract. Everton signed the contract.

"At the last moment, the players decided not to sign. And basically, Balogun's allegation is that I'm not feeling well because of the way the club treated me. I'm not feeling well because Everton's medical department raised doubts about my future or my health. I have nothing (no health problem), so I'm not comfortable signing a long contract here. And that's the way we finish our transfer window."

All the while, with Monaco in need of funds and Balogun failing his medical, Monaco agreed to sell Lamine Camara to Chelsea, with the Blues on the lookout for a replacement for Enzo Fernandez, who moved to Manchester City for $169.1 million earlier that day.

But when Everton approved Balogun's medical, Monaco called off the sale of Camara - only then for the American to pull out of the move.

"So basically, the story about those two players and what happened yesterday was also new for me," Scuro noted. "It's the first time in my career that I saw a last day (deadline day) like this.

"It's not nice to stay the last two days of the transfer window until 3 a.m. in the office, trying to find solutions here and there. And this is something that we need to try to do better as a club, because it puts everyone in a situation where what is happening can happen. And it's not nice to be here, having to explain and having to face all the consequences of this.

• Manchester City sign Everton's Iliman Ndiaye for $88 million after Cody Gakpo move fails

"And the reality is now that we are very, very happy that Lamine stayed. We want to be strong on the pitch. We want to grow this season, and we are going for that. And now we are still waiting for 'Balo' to come back for us to sit and discuss and to realize between us what's next.

"We still have other markets open, which we are having discussions about with different players, including 'Balo'. Let's see what can still happen until Thursday, because we still have markets that have the financial capacity to do something. And this is what happened, and this is where we are today."

title: Are Arsenal taking a risk in not signing a world-class forward?
description: Arsenal have been busy in the transfer market as they look to defend their Premier League title, but do they lack a world class striker still?
fullText:
"Very ambitious, very fast, and very smart."

That was manager Mikel Arteta's aim for Arsenal's transfer dealings following their defeat by Paris St-Germain in the Champions League final in May.

The Gunners won their first title in 22 years last season by seven points and did not lose a game in the Champions League during normal time, with their only loss in the competition coming to Luis Enrique's side on penalties.

But it was clear coming into the summer transfer window that the club were looking for a game-changing attacker to lift their forward line.

Viktor Gyokeres - a £64m signing last summer from Portuguese side Sporting - scored 21 goals in his first season for Arsenal but his performances still raised questions about whether he is the best fit for Arteta's side going forward.

The same debate was posed on the left wing with Leandro Trossard's form dipping after starting the season well and Gabriel Martinelli, despite scoring six goals in the Champions League campaign, scoring just once in the league.

And now both of those players have left the club.

But finding an attacker who could elevate a squad that almost won a domestic and European double proved difficult.

Arsenal want to be one of the best clubs in the world.

In an interview with the Times, chief executive Richard Garlick said that joining the world's super-clubs is "the goal - that's the ambition".

In that same interview, Garlick acknowledged that the "pool of players is smaller now than it was a few years ago if we're going to improve".

And unfortunately for the Gunners, they have found that out this summer.

Sporting director Andrea Berta is known for speaking to multiple targets at once while preparing the deals simultaneously.

The Gunners went into this window with interest in Morgan Rogers, Bradley Barcola, Julian Alvarez and Vinicius Jr.

Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius Jr turned public and was shaped around his contract situation at Real Madrid.

Ultimately, the Spanish club offered him a bigger package than they had done before Arsenal's interest stepped up.

But inside the club, there was a period where they thought they were going to be successful in bringing one of the best wingers in world football to north London.

Questions will be posed as to why the club did not go big for Rogers, but Arsenal stuck to their valuation of £80m before Chelsea then paid £117m for the former Aston Villa forward.

That left Julian Alvarez as the only available target in the window after Liverpool succeeded in bringing in Bradley Barcola.

Arsenal always had reservations about paying the fee needed to get Barcola too.

It appeared Alvarez's only way out of Atletico Madrid was Arsenal, after Atleti were adamant that they would not negotiate with Barcelona.

However, Alvarez returned to training with the Spanish side and, despite Arteta's best efforts laying out plans to the player, the deal did not come off.

Arteta joins elite 250 club - but where does he rank?

Arsenal's Nwaneri joins Dortmund on loan

Arsenal showed the strength of their squad in their win over Aston Villa on Monday night.

They brought in Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes for £75m, Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa (£55m), turned Piero Hincapie's loan deal into a permanent one (£34.5m) and signed Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge for £34m.

Tzolis struggled in the win but has already impressed in the Community Shield victory over Manchester City and the opening day Premier League win over Coventry.

Guimaraes is being described by some as one of the signings of the window, and Konsa was statistically the best defender in the league for ground duel success (73.1%) and passing accuracy (95%) last season.

Konsa, although he brings the number of senior defenders in Arsenal's squad to eight, was brought in because of the injuries to William Saliba and Jurrien Timber.

A big part of Arsenal's window has been who they have let go too.

Gabriel Martinelli is close to completing a move for around £60m to Al-Hilal, which would be a record sale for the club.

Leandro Trossard has moved to Besiktas (£15.3m), while Christian Norgaard was sold to Everton (£7m).

The main worry from supporters is that they have let two forwards go who play on the left wing and brought in just one to replace them.

There is no denying that Arsenal wanted a game-changing attacker this summer - if there was one available.

Not signing one this window does leave them with the chance to act again in January or wait completely until next summer to try to bring in a new forward.

But there will be uncomfortable conversations about why there hasn't been one during this window, even if the football leadership team are content with the business the club has done.

Questions will of course be asked of Arteta, Berta and co-chair Josh Kroenke as to why, after Arsenal's success, such an attractive club weren't able to get one of their targets over the line.

However, there is no denying that Arsenal's squad is one of the best in Europe. Their bench for the win over Aston Villa contained nine full internationals with two of those - Merino and Zubimendi - World Cup winners.

Gabriel Jesus has moved to Barcelona for £12.8m, and although he was not an integral part of Arsenal's team because of selection and fitness issues, he still made 27 appearances in all competitions, scoring six goals.

With Martinelli and Trossard both gone, there will be more opportunity for Eberechi Eze to play from the left wing, a position he shone in at former club Crystal Palace.

Eze played in some of the biggest games of Arsenal's last campaign on the left wing and put in an impressive appearance in that role in the win over Villa on Monday too.

Last season, Kai Havertz missed large parts of the campaign with injury, while Mikel Merino, another option to play at striker, missed a chunk of the season too but both have started this season fully fit.

Those injuries last season meant that Gyokeres had to lead the line for long periods without back-up in his first campaign with Arsenal, but despite that test, it does not take away that the Swedish international's suitability is still in question.

It is also intriguing that Gyokeres has not played a minute of the opening two Premier League matches so far.

Arsenal are still looking like the early season favourites and have the potential to defend their title, but criticism surrounding the lack of a new forward will be tough to avoid if goals start to become hard to come by.

title: Premier League breaks transfer record for second straight summer
description: Premier League clubs break their all-time summer transfer record after spending reaches £3.198bn.
fullText:
Premier League clubs have broken their all-time summer transfer record after spending reached £3.46bn.

English top flight clubs had already pushed well beyond the £3bn barrier when Iliman Ndiaye's move from Everton to Manchester City on deadline day for an initial £60m took the amount spent past the previous mark of £3.14bn from 12 months ago.

Enzo Fernandez's move from Chelsea to Manchester City for a joint-British transfer record fee of £125m was then confirmed shortly after the transfer window closed.

A total of £475m was spent on deadline day itself, up from £391m last year.

The total amount spent during the window considerably dwarfs the £1.13bn spent by clubs just five years ago and underlines the power top English clubs have to attract talent, according to figures provided to BBC Sport by Paul Macdonald, founder of FootballTransfers.com.

Follow live coverage of transfer deadline day
